deep.reconstruction:
Setting (taken from p.270 and checked for consistency). The page concerns the Snellius–Pothenot resection problem. A, B, C are the three known stations and P is the observer (the '4th point'). a=BC, b=CA, c=AB are the sides of triangle ABC, and alpha=PA, beta=PB, gamma=PC.

The rays PA, PB, PC split the vertex angles:
- at A: 1=∠PAC and 2=∠PAB;
- at B: 3=∠PBA and 4=∠PBC;
- at C: 5=∠PCB and 6=∠PCA.
Hence A=1+2, B=3+4, C=5+6.

The observed angles at P are 𝔄=∠BPC=180°−(4+5), 𝔅=∠CPA=180°−(6+1) and ℭ=∠APB=180°−(2+3).

Equation (1) is 1+2+3+4+5+6=180° (Fig. I, P inside the triangle). Equation (2) is the trigonometric Ceva relation sin1·sin3·sin5 = sin2·sin4·sin6. Equations (3)–(11) on p.270 are its consequences. They give 𝔄−A=3+6, 𝔅−B=2+5 and ℭ−C=1+4.

This page: geometric meaning of (2)–(11) via five circles.

(i) The law of sines in triangle ABC, whose circumdiameter is p, gives sinA=a/p, sinB=b/p, sinC=c/p.

(ii) Triangle PBC has angle 𝔄 at P (opposite a), angle 4 at B (opposite gamma) and angle 5 at C (opposite beta). With circumdiameter q: sin𝔄=a/q, sin4=gamma/q, sin5=beta/q.

(iii) Triangle PCA, with circumdiameter r: sin𝔅=b/r, sin6=alpha/r, sin1=gamma/r.

(iv) Triangle PAB, with circumdiameter s: sinℭ=c/s, sin2=beta/s, sin3=alpha/s.

(v) The fifth circle is circumscribed about Fig. II, a triangle whose sides are proportional to aα, bβ, cγ and whose angles are 𝔄−A, 𝔅−B, ℭ−C. This is my identification: it is similar to the pedal triangle of P, whose sides are α·sinA = aα/(2R), and to the inverse of ABC in P. Its diameter t then gives sin(𝔄−A)=aα/t, sin(𝔅−B)=bβ/t, sin(ℭ−C)=cγ/t.
- Here t has the dimension of an area.
- Comparing with the 'Viereckgleichungen' of p.270 gives t = 2αβγR/(R²−ρ²), where R=p/2 and ρ=|PO| (my inference).

Substituting these 15 sine values into the 10 equations (2)–(11) makes each an identity in a,b,c,α,β,γ,p,q,r,s,t. Examples (my verification):
- (2): (γ/r)(α/s)(β/q) = (β/s)(γ/q)(α/r).
- (4): sin1·sinB·sin𝔄 = sin4·sinA·sin𝔅 becomes (γ/r)(b/p)(a/q) = (γ/q)(a/p)(b/r).
- (3): sin1·sinℭ·sin(𝔅−B) = sin2·sin(ℭ−C)·sin𝔅 becomes (γ/r)(c/s)(bβ/t) = (β/s)(cγ/t)(b/r).

Second part: symmetry of the system. Equation (3), sin1·sin(2+3)·sin(2+5) = sin2·sin(1+4)·sin(1+6), is multiplied by −1 on both sides: sin(−1)·sin(2+3)·sin(2+5) = sin(−2)·sin(1+4)·sin(1+6).

The six quantities x1'=−1, x3'=2+3, x5'=2+5, x2'=−2, x4'=1+4, x6'=1+6 satisfy the same hypotheses as 1,3,5;2,4,6:
- their sum is 1+2+3+4+5+6=180°, which is (1);
- the displayed equation is exactly (2) for them.

Hence every consequence derived from (1),(2) transfers. Each of (3)–(11) can serve as the starting equation from which the other nine follow. Geometrically, this substitution (an involution) corresponds to interchanging the role of P with a vertex of the complete quadrangle ABCP.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page; all 15 sine formulas are correct law-of-sines statements under the stated labeling, and the substitution check works.
Fig. II is not described on this page. The identification of t's triangle (sides ∝ aα, bβ, cγ, angles 𝔄−A etc.) is inferred from the formulas and from p.270.
On p.270 the transcription shows slips in (6) ('sin([-4-]2+5)') and (11) ('sin(6+7)' should be sin(6+3)). These are not on this page.

results.what: Sines of all 15 angles of the Pothenot configuration expressed as chord/diameter in five circles (circumcircles of ABC, PBC, PCA, PAB and of a triangle with sides aα, bβ, cγ)
results.modern_name: Law of sines (extended) applied to the complete quadrangle
Trigonometric Ceva theorem and its quadrangle variants

results.what: Triangle with sides aα, bβ, cγ having angles 𝔄−A, 𝔅−B, ℭ−C, circumdiameter t = 2αβγR/(R²−ρ²)
results.modern_name: Pedal triangle / inversion triangle (Ptolemy inequality triangle); pedal circumradius αβγ/(2(R²−ρ²))
results.usually_credited_to: 19th-century triangle geometry (pedal triangle properties; Euler/Gergonne-type relations)

results.what: Substitution 1→−1, 2→−2, 3→2+3, 4→1+4, 5→2+5, 6→1+6 preserves (1),(2), so any of the ten equations generates the rest
results.modern_name: Symmetry of the complete quadrangle (interchange of the fourth point with a vertex)

deep.surprise_reason: This is an elegant but elementary treatment of the Pothenot problem by Ceva-type sine relations and the law of sines. The pedal-triangle circle is a nice touch, but all of it is classical triangle geometry, and Gauss's work on the Pothenot problem is known in connection with his geodesy.

transcription_corrections: Line 2 of formulas: the manuscript reads sin𝔄 = a/q (Latin a, side BC), not α/q. This is required by the law of sines in triangle PBC.
'sin ℭ = c/s': the denominator is a (somewhat overwritten) s; correct as transcribed.
'denselben Bedingungen': the correction of 'de-' to 'den-' is fine; the manuscript shows 'denselben' with an overwrite.
